query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during L-PBF processing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder reduces thermal gradients, thereby mitigating compositional segregation, residual stress accumulation, and defect formation, which in turn improves mechanical integrity compared with conventional room-temperature processing.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock processed via conventional L-PBF conditions that are prone to rapid cooling, segregation, high residual stress, and defect formation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a substrate preheating step (e.g., raising the build platform temperature to around 200°C) during the L-PBF fabrication process.
generation.conditions: Maintain optimized laser power and scanning speed parameters within typical L-PBF processing settings; the intervention is valid under energy densities that produce near-full density parts (approximately >99%) while avoiding excessive thermal input.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients and a slower cooling rate during solidification.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate decreases the temperature differential between the molten pool and the substrate, which lowers the cooling rate. This reduction mitigates the formation of residual stresses, minimizes elemental segregation during rapid solidification, and reduces the likelihood of defect (such as hot cracking) formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples fabricated with substrate preheating will exhibit lower residual stress measurements, more homogeneous microstructures with reduced segregation, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., higher tensile strength and toughness) relative to samples produced without preheating.
generation.baseline: Conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi samples via L-PBF using a room-temperature substrate, which tend to show higher thermal gradients, pronounced segregation, and increased hot-cracking.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective within standard L-PBF parameter ranges and moderate preheat temperatures (e.g., up to about 400°C). Results might vary outside these processing conditions and could be less effective if energy densities are substantially beyond typical values or if thermal management is otherwise altered.
generation.uncertainty: While qualitative improvements in microstructural homogeneity and reduced defects are anticipated, precise quantitative gains in mechanical strength and stress reduction are uncertain and may depend on careful tuning of the preheat temperature and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of AlCrFeNiSi samples using L-PBF under identical laser power and scanning speed: one group with the build substrate preheated (e.g., 200°C) and the other with a room-temperature substrate. Ensure all other processing parameters remain constant.
measurements: Microstructural analysis for segregation using SEM/EDS
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant reductions in residual stresses and segregation, or if they do not exhibit improved mechanical properties compared to the control group, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Laser Powder Bed Fusion Additive Manufacturing of a CoCrFeNiCu High-Entropy Alloy: Processability, Microstructural Insights, and (In Situ) Mechanical Behavior

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys are known for their promising mechanical properties, wear and corrosion resistance, which are maintained across a wide range of temperatures. In this study, a CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloy, distinguished from conventional CoCrFeNi systems by the addition of Cu, which is known to enhance toughness and wear resistance, was investigated to better understand the effects of compositional modification on processability and performance. The influence of key process parameters, specifically laser power and scan speed, on the processability of CoCrFeNiCu-based high-entropy alloys produced by laser powder bed fusion additive manufacturing was investigated, with a focus of low laser power, which is critical for minimizing defects and improving the resulting microstructure and mechanical performance. Nonequilibrium chemical short-range order in metallic alloys

Abstract: AbstractMetallic alloys are routinely subjected to nonequilibrium processes during manufacturing, such as rapid solidification and thermomechanical processing. It has been suggested in the high-entropy alloy literature that chemical short-range order (SRO) could offer a new knob to tailor materials properties. While evidence of the effect of SRO on materials properties accumulates, the state of SRO evolution during alloy manufacturing remains obscure. Here, we employ high-fidelity atomistic simulations to track SRO evolution during the solidification and thermomechanical processing of alloys. Our investigation reveals that alloy processing can lead to nonequilibrium steady-states of SRO that are different from any equilibrium state. The mechanism behind nonequilibrium SRO formation is shown to be an inherent ordering bias present in nonequilibrium events. These results demonstrate that conventional manufacturing processes provide pathways for tuning SRO that lead to a broad nonequilibrium spectrum of SRO states beyond the equilibrium design space of alloys.Subject terms: Atomistic models, Metals and alloys This
